# Benchmarks

Numbers Hormozi gives, with context. Generated from BENCHMARK atoms and from the `numbers:` line of every other atom — do not edit by hand.
A number that appears in a single recording may be a transcription error; check the source before relying on it.

| EXAMPLE | Giveaway examples across business types pair a high-value grand prize with a voucher or partial version as the promotional offer. | Braces $6,000 / $2,000 card; dog food $1,000 / $300 card; services $5,000 / $2,000 voucher; consulting $12,000. | [MM-12@00:14:34] |
| TACTIC | Give away two grand prizes — one to the winner and one to whoever referred them — to make every entrant recruit others, multiplying leads. | Can double, triple or quadruple giveaway leads. | [MM-12@00:17:40] |
| TACTIC | Limit entries by time, by count, or both, and set the cap by how many leads your team can actually contact. | Example caps: 7 days; 5,000 entries; 200 leads when contact capacity is limited. | [MM-12@00:18:35] |
| TACTIC | In recurring-revenue businesses, spread the promotional discount across the longest commitment they will accept and auto-bill at full price afterwards — never as free months up front. | $8,000/year service − $2,000 credit = $6,000 → $500/month for 12 months, then $8,000/12 (~$667/month). | [MM-12@00:21:49] |
| CASE | Mentor John's 22 tanning salons used a $5 five-day VIP pass that converted most visitors into $19.99/month memberships once they learned one session can't give a real tan. | $5 pass; $25/session vs $19.99/month unlimited. | [MM-13@00:00:00] |
| CASE | When Gym Launch's ads stopped working, a "Free 21-Day Transformation" decoy beat every tested offer, with most people choosing the premium. | 5 beta groups; 10–15 lb in 21 days guarantee. | [MM-13@00:01:35] |
| DEFINITION | A decoy offer advertises something free or discounted; when leads ask about it, you present a far more valuable premium offer beside it, so everyone buys one or the other. | 70–80% of leads should take the premium when structured properly. | [MM-13@00:03:38] |
| TACTIC | When someone takes the decoy, surprise them with a few low-cost premium features — it builds goodwill, proves your sincerity, and creates the next sales moment. | ~$300 supplement sale at the bonus consult. | [MM-13@00:12:25] |
| CASE | Nashville's Boot Factory sold "buy one pair, get two free" by pricing three pairs into the first — and bachelorette parties bought in groups. | $600 for one + two free = $200/pair. | [MM-14@00:01:37] |
| DEFINITION | In Buy X Get Y Free, customers buy something to get other things free, which turns a discount into a far stronger "free" offer while still selling full-priced units. | 33% off ≡ buy two get one free. | [MM-14@00:02:24] |
| EXAMPLE | T-shirt math: Buy X Get Y can be a pure reframe or a reframe on top of a discount. | $10/shirt reframe; $6.67/shirt with discount. | [MM-14@00:03:37] |
| EXAMPLE | 18 months of service for $1,800 converts best framed as "buy 6, get 12 free". | 18 months for $1,800 in all versions. | [MM-14@00:05:45] |
| DECISION_RULE | Don't sell long prepayments if you can't manage cash or need the money to survive, and cap annual prepay at about 10% of recurring customers. | Cap at ~10% of recurring base (e.g., 10 of 100). | [MM-14@00:09:00] |
| TACTIC | Size the package beyond your normal customer lifespan so the offer extends how long customers pay. | 3-month norm → 4-month package ≈ 33% more revenue per customer. | [MM-14@00:12:53] |
| CASE | A speed-reading trainer sold "double your reading speed in three hours or it's free": $0 down and $300 billed after, a $97 pay-now option, and an eight-week intensive pitched at the end. | $0/$300 later; $97 now with recordings; 3-hour training; 8-week back end. | [MM-15@00:00:00] |
| FRAMEWORK | Make three offers in order: pay later (free today, full price afterwards), pay now (discount plus bonuses), then an upsell. | Pay-now discount 20–50%, sometimes ~67%. | [MM-15@00:06:19] |
| PRINCIPLE | Get just enough pay-now buyers to cover acquisition cost, then let as many as possible take pay-later at about three times the price. | Pay-later ≈ 3× pay-now; break even within 30 days. | [MM-15@00:04:36] |
| EXAMPLE | Real-estate workshop: free three-day "find your first deal" billed $500 after, $299 now with bonuses, and a $30,000 upsell. | $500 later; $299 now; $30,000 upsell. | [MM-15@00:06:19] |
| EXAMPLE | Physical product: a 14-day clothing trial billed after if kept, a cheaper pay-now price with an accessory, and a subscription upsell. | ~$148–149 later vs ~$97 now (unclear in audio). | [MM-15@00:07:09] |
| EXAMPLE | Local service: lawn and hedge work paid after if satisfied, a cheaper pay-now bundle with lawn treatment, then a monthly lawn-care upsell. | ~$600 vs ~$369 (illustrative); $199/month upsell. | [MM-15@00:07:55] |
| DECISION_RULE | Balance the options by adjusting pay-now incentives, and expect about 10% of pay-later buyers to cancel — more signals a problem. | ~10% expected cancellations. | [MM-15@00:10:17] |
| TACTIC | Subscriptions: free trial at the higher rate, then a thank-you-page offer to skip the trial and lock in a lower rate for life. | $400/month trial rate vs $300/month locked for life. | [MM-15@00:11:02] |
| DEFINITION | Free with Consumption gives away valuable education — 20 minutes to 5 days long — that breaks the prospect's beliefs, then offers what solves their next concern. | 20 minutes to 5 days of consumption. | [MM-16@00:01:39] |
| CASE | Chiropractors' free diabetic/neuropathy dinners sell a cheap consult in a 90-minute talk, then a year-long program — about 10% of diners buy the big offer. | 25% → consult; 1/3 → program; ≈8–10% of attendees; 100 diners × 10 × $10K ≈ $100K. | [MM-16@00:06:07] |
| TACTIC | Beginners can run it one-to-one: five one-hour sessions toward a goal, permission on day one to make an offer at the end, then the pitch. | 5 × 1-hour sessions; ~$3,000/year probe; ~20 conversations. | [MM-16@00:09:11] |
| EXAMPLE | A burger shop earning $0.25 on a $2 burger reaches about $1.75 gross profit per sale with fries, soda and supersizing. | $2 price, $1.75 cost; $0.25 → $1.75 per sale (called 8×; figures give 7×). | [MM-17@00:01:32] |
| CASE | A fourth-generation furrier lured customers with free fur earmuffs, then sold summer coat storage and conditioning — about $1.4M a summer. | ~$200 × ~7,000 coats ≈ $1.4M; ~$30 to store earmuffs. | [MM-18@00:00:00] |
| CASE | Gym prospects who refused every service got a free at-home program and nutrition consult — and there bought supplements at a higher ticket than members. | Avg supplement ticket $200 (service buyers) vs $300 (non-buyers). | [MM-18@00:02:12] |
| CASE | A storage-facility owner showed that a "free month of storage" is worth about $127 once the required lock, boxes, hand trucks, insurance and larger units are sold. | ~$127 per free month; lock $47; insurance +$10/month at ~90% margin. | [MM-18@00:05:18] |
| EXAMPLE | Vertical examples: supplements at weight-loss orientation, recovery products after free physio, and free coaching tied to required software. | Orientation supplement sale typically covered CAC. | [MM-18@00:08:05] |
| CASE | A weight-loss chain charged about $5/month for doctor-supervised services and made its money on roughly $5,000 of supplements and food sold on day two. | ~$5/month services; ~$5,000 supplements on day two. | [MM-18@00:08:57] |
| BENCHMARK | 80%+ of buyers should take a classic upsell; around 30% means it isn't presented as assumed enough. | Target ≥80% uptake; ~30% = not assumed. | [MM-18@00:13:18] |
| CASE | After going 0-for-19 pitching supplement science, a worn-out Hormozi simply asked a customer which flavours she wanted and charged her card on file — and then closed everyone else that day. | $5,000 initial inventory; friend at ~$80K/month; ~70% female clientele; 0 for 19 → closed ~12 in a row. | [MM-19@00:00:48] |
| CASE | Writing one talkative client a detailed regimen led the next client to ask for "what you did for her" — and buying everything with no pitch at all revealed the prescription close. | $5,000–10,000/day in supplement sales; 48 consults/day (4 people per hour, in pairs). | [MM-19@00:03:50] |
| CASE | Running out of stock and pointing a customer to buy some items elsewhere made her buy everything else effortlessly — so Hormozi started keeping products specifically to cross off. | Fish oil ~$3 margin vs fat burner ~$40 margin. | [MM-19@00:06:25] |
| TACTIC | When stock is low, nudge toward what you have; when sold out or at capacity, still take payment and set a clear later delivery or start date — then beat it. | Promise 7 days; 4 = happy, 10 = angry; at-capacity service start delayed 14 days. | [MM-19@00:14:16] |
| CASE | Hormozi entered a suit shop with a $500 budget, was shown a $16,000 suit first, and happily left having spent about $2,500–3,000. | Budget $500; anchor $16,000; spent ≈ $2,500–3,000. | [MM-20@00:00:22] |
| PRINCIPLE | Anchors pay twice: main-offer buyers spend more than planned, and a minority buy the premium — one in ten buying a 10× offer doubles revenue. | 1 in 5 at $16K ≈ +$3,000 per sale; 1 in 10 at 10× = 2× revenue. | [MM-20@00:05:10] |
| DECISION_RULE | The anchor must be an order of magnitude higher — 5–10× — and no gasp means it wasn't high enough or wasn't sold earnestly. | Anchor 5–10× main; main at roughly 1/5–1/10 of anchor. | [MM-20@00:06:01] |
| EXAMPLE | Lawn care: a $1,000/week package with the owner's cell, fancy mulch and natural pest control makes the $200/week standard an easy yes — a price that used to get haggled down. | $1,000 vs $200/week; ~80% indifferent. | [MM-20@00:07:32] |
| CASE | Hormozi's gym applied Win Your Money Back credit as free months and members quit; a friend kept most paying by rolling winnings into a year. | $150/month; $600 = 4 free months. | [MM-21@00:00:00] |
| TACTIC | Gift-card play: sell $200 gift cards for $20, usable only by someone else, then roll each redeemed card into an offer worth at least 5× its value. | $200 card for $20; next offer ≥ $1,000, e.g., $2,000. | [MM-21@00:09:07] |
| BENCHMARK | Most times, adding third-party financing raises revenue by about 35% on average (Hormozi's figure) — typically worth the setup work. | +35% revenue on average from adding third-party financing. | [MM-23@00:04:35] |
| CASE | At Allen (software), agency owners who wanted to pay a $20,000 onboarding at $800 every other week paid it off within a month once told they could fly in only after paying. | $20,000 price; proposed $800 every two weeks; actual payoff ~1 month. | [MM-23@00:06:47] |
| TACTIC | Steps 5–6: drop to a third down with two later payments, then spread payments evenly — but still front-load, since you already paid to acquire and onboard the customer. | Gym Launch 16 weekly charges for a 16-week programme. | [MM-23@00:10:39] |
| CASE | Gym Launch chose its HR platform because the vendor charged $500 and rebated it if Layla attended the onboarding trainings — and then kept the account for years. | $500 charge, rebated after 2–3 training sessions. | [MM-24@00:00:00] |
| BENCHMARK | Illustration: closing 3 of 10 on the attraction offer, downselling 4 more to a trial and upselling 3 of those afterwards doubles customers from 3 to 6. | 3/10 closed → +4 trials → +3 upsold = 6 customers (2x). | [MM-24@00:02:19] |
| EXAMPLE | Trial-with-penalty terms for consumer, business and therapy offers. | 100 outbound messages/day; $50 fee per miss (therapy). | [MM-24@00:04:25] |
| TACTIC | Size fees so they add up to what the win-your-money-back offer would have cost, weighting the most important actions higher. | $500 / 10 actions = $50; consults $100–150; minor $25. | [MM-24@00:05:30] |
| TACTIC | If asking for a card on a free trial feels awkward, charge a token amount up front — it justifies the card and confirms it works before recurring billing. | $1 first month or $10 down. | [MM-24@00:18:48] |
| CASE | A friend raised his close rate from 25% to 75% by offering his $4,000 programme for $2,000 without the guarantee — many then chose the full-price version. | Per 100 prospects: before 25 bought at $4,000; after 35 bought at $4,000 and 40 took the $2,000 version (25% → 75% close). | [MM-25@00:00:00] |
| FRAMEWORK | Standard order: first remove something valuable for a small price cut to push them back to the original; if that fails, restore it and remove things they don't value for a big cut; keep going until they buy. | Example step 1: $4,000 → $3,500 without guarantee. | [MM-25@00:08:37] |
| EXAMPLE | Selling a $1,000 product as $50/month can bring in four times the buyers and the same per-customer revenue, at the cost of far less cash up front. | 10 × $1,000 = $10k vs 40 × $50 × 20 months = $40k; 4x customers. | [MM-26@00:00:00] |
| TACTIC | Downsell the upsell: after a short, high-priced front offer, sell a longer commitment with more value at a lower weekly or monthly rate. | $16,000/16 weeks; $600/6 weeks → $200/month. | [MM-26@00:01:35] |
| FRAMEWORK | Big head, long tail: charge a large upfront payment followed by a small recurring fee — customers protect the low rate they "bought", so churn is tiny. | $100 + $10/mo vs $19.99/mo; $1,000 + $50/mo vs $200/mo; $5,000 + $200/mo. | [MM-26@00:05:43] |
| CASE | A course creator advertised "all my courses free" — $24,000 of real-priced products — for starting a free 30-day trial of his $399/month newsletter, then upsold a lifetime rate on the thank-you page. | $24,000 bonus value; $399/month after 30 days free; $299/month lifetime if paid today. | [MM-27@00:00:00] |
| DEFINITION | A continuity bonus offer gives the customer something great for signing up to continuity today — typically worth more than the first continuity payment. | Gym challenge $600–800 vs $200/month membership (first figure unclear in audio). | [MM-27@00:03:24] |
| EXAMPLE | Continuity bonus examples for physical, service and digital businesses — one-time bonuses get them to buy, recurring bonuses get them to stay. | $59/mo + $800 toys; $1,000 accelerator with $100/mo; $15,800 back issues, $399 vs $299/mo. | [MM-27@00:06:08] |
| BENCHMARK | In tested gym sales, people paid about a 33% premium to avoid continuity: a standalone price 1.33x the monthly continuity price split buyers 50/50. | 1.33x/50%, 1.66x/60%, 2x/70%, 2.3x/80%, 2.66x/90%, 3x/~100%. | [MM-27@00:14:56] |
| BENCHMARK | A bulk prepay upsell on continuity ("buy five months, get one free") lifts 30-day cash by 50% if only one in eight members takes it. | 1 in 8 taking buy-5-get-1 → +50% 30-day profit. | [MM-27@00:18:10] |
| TACTIC | Pair the bonus with a commitment — free only if they join for 3, 6 or 12 months — trading fewer takers for locked-in term. | $500 bonus for $1,200 (6 months) or $2,400 (12 months) commitment. | [MM-27@00:18:57] |
| CASE | Hormozi's Austin neighbour built and sold a waste-management company by offering apartment complexes a free year of service for signing five-year agreements. | 1 free year + 5 paid years. | [MM-28@00:00:00] |
| TACTIC | Never let free months eat into the committed term: "three months free with a year" means 3 free plus 12 paid, not 3 plus 9. | 12 vs 9 paid months = +33%. | [MM-28@00:03:07] |
| TACTIC | Spread the discount across the term — advertise the total as free months or a credit, then deduct it evenly from each payment. | $600 over 12 months → $150 instead of $200 per month. | [MM-28@00:04:39] |
| TACTIC | Deliver the free time as a physical gift card redeemable after the first few payments — every outcome is good for the business. | Redeemable after the first 3 payments (example). | [MM-28@00:11:39] |
| CASE | A consultant running a ~$5M/year no-employee lifestyle business keeps almost every client on payment plans by waiving a $25,000 onboarding fee for those who commit to a year. | $25,000 fee; $4,000/month; 12-month commitment; ~$5M/year. | [MM-29@00:00:00] |
| DEFINITION | A waived-fee offer charges month-to-month customers a startup fee of 3–5x the monthly rate and waives it for those who commit to a long term — unless they cancel early. | Fee 3–5x monthly (e.g., $5,000 on $1,000/month); term ≥6, ideally 12+ months. | [MM-29@00:02:17] |
| EXAMPLE | Hormozi's favourite version — fee with commitment — on a $1,000/month service with a $5,000 fee and a 12-month term. | $1,000/month, $5,000 fee, 12 months. | [MM-29@00:04:30] |
| FRAMEWORK | The waived-fee offer has four levers — commitment length, committed rate, month-to-month rate and the fee — that can be mixed freely; default to a fee of 5x the monthly price. | Default fee = 5x monthly price. | [MM-29@00:05:15] |
| DECISION_RULE | Size the fee by your goal: a larger fee pushes more people to commit; a smaller one (1.5–3x monthly) pushes more to month-to-month and brings more cash up front. | Cash-focused fee 1.5–3x monthly; commitment-focused 3–5x. | [MM-29@00:07:41] |
| EXAMPLE | The newsletter model used a free trial as the attraction offer and a pay-less-now/lifetime-discount combination to make it cash-flow; Hormozi would add a bulk prepay only if retention were short. | $399/month; buy 6 get 6 sensible when average remaining stay ~3 months. | [MM-30@00:02:17] |
| DEFINITION | A money model is a purposeful sequence of offers that increases the number of customers, the amount each pays and the speed of payment; a good one earns more profit within 30 days than it costs to acquire and serve the customer. | Allen $0 → $1.7M/month in 6 months; Gym Launch $0 → $4.4M/month in 20 months. | [MM-31@00:00:00] |
| BENCHMARK | Hormozi typically prices the backend upsell at about five times the core offer; if 20% of customers take it, revenue doubles. | 100 customers × $1,000 = $100K; 20 of them × $5,000 = another $100K → revenue doubled. | [SC-08@00:01:35] |
| EXAMPLE | Applied to a marketing agency, the Crazy Eight turns into price rises, lower churn, cheaper delivery, added services, senior access, longer contracts and lighter versions. | One rep servicing 10 clients instead of 5 doubles margin; ~78% of businesses are services. | [SC-08@00:04:49] |
| CASE | A consumer service business in the portfolio, stuck without a backend offer at this stage, was turned into a SaaS business and grew to over $100M run rate. | LTV 2x then +50%; >$100M annual run rate; valued ~$350M conservatively, possibly $500–600M depending on buyer. | [SC-08@00:24:00] |

| EXAMPLE | Price the front end above the ongoing membership to recoup ad cost, then drop buyers into a lower recurring rate that feels like a deal. | $2,000 for 12 weeks (about $650-$700/month); follow-on $399-$499/month. | [POD-0002@00:08:55] |

| TACTIC | If you give away free time to try your service, sell something for roughly $500 to $700 on the front end when people come in. | Front-end price $500-$700; 10-15 new customers a week for the challenge model. | [POD-0063@00:10:07] |

| CASE | Recommending landing-page software to customers earned about $724,000 in commissions. | $724,000 total commissions. | [POD-0169@00:05:05] |
| BENCHMARK | Three of four Americans buy a dietary supplement, and the average gym or affiliate sold supplements to about 14 people a month. | 74% of Americans use at least one supplement; 14 supplement sales per month per gym. | [POD-0169@00:01:27] |
| EXAMPLE | His first supplement sale came when he stopped explaining ingredients and asked "chocolate or vanilla?" | friend's store about $75,000 a month. | [POD-0170@00:03:26] |
| EXAMPLE | A new rental-car clerk added about $400 to his booking with a short script of choice-framed upsells. | about $400 added to the ticket; prepaid tank about 25 gallons at roughly $3 = about $75; insurance about $20/day. | [POD-0172@00:02:26] |
| TACTIC | At sign-up, sell the member through to their goal (for example 36 weeks) instead of a membership or free trial. | about 36 weeks, about $2,000 sale; 2x to 3x the average gym's lifetime value. | [POD-0172@00:08:37] |
| BENCHMARK | At a nutrition orientation after sign-up, about 80% buy at least two supplements and a third to a half take meals. | about 80% buy 2 or more supplements; 1 in 3 to 1 in 2 take 1 to 3 meals a day (depends on the salesperson). | [POD-0172@00:09:22] |
| TACTIC | Step down in order: pay in full on a card, smaller down payment with weekly payments, a short fixed term, then a free trial with commitments. | Example ladder: $3,000 prepay; $1,000 down with 10% off and $66 a week instead of $99; 6 or 12 weeks for $600 with no further payments. | [POD-0182@00:05:14] |
| EXAMPLE | In the free-trial step the client initials a short list of commitments, with a small fee per miss. | 8 workouts and 3 appointments in 21 days; $25 fee per miss. | [POD-0182@00:05:59] |
| TACTIC | Run internal sales plays to existing clients at least four times a year and take that profit out. | At least 4 plays per year. | [POD-0184@00:13:18] |
| TACTIC | Set the gap between the two options by your goal: a very high option A pushes people into continuity; equal prices push cash up front. | Option A $500-$700 for ~90% continuity take-up; equal prices for cash up front. | [POD-0196@00:08:51] |
| TACTIC | Step two: start on the card they have with a small amount, and swap in the preferred card for the rest. | Example: instead of a $300 sale, start with $49 on the card at hand. | [POD-0204@00:01:33] |
| TACTIC | Step three: start them with the card they have, delay the charge about two days, and swap the card at orientation. | Delay: 2 days. | [POD-0204@00:02:23] |
| TACTIC | Fastest cash: text existing customers a reason-why offer with very few spots, for example three people for a one-year transformation at $3,000. | 3 spots x $3,000 = $9,000; about 3 takers per 100 customers. | [YT-SvIcS-Q1Hl4@00:04:20] |

| TACTIC | For more money, give the challenge away free to members and upsell food and supplements, which reaches about 85% take rate and 80-90% closing on the upsell. | 85% take, 80-90% upsell close; $10,000-$20,000 per month; item bought at about $5, sold at $20. | [YT-SvIcS-Q1Hl4@00:06:41] |
| DECISION_RULE | Match the play to how fast you need cash: tomorrow means a paid-in-full text blast, two weeks means an internal apply/promotion, and if you can wait a month you should probably do the free-then-upsell hybrid. | Hybrid: $144,000 top line; $120,000 bottom line. | [YT-SvIcS-Q1Hl4@00:11:04] |

## retention-ltv

| type | claim | numbers | source |
|---|---|---|---|
| EXAMPLE | Activation points in Hormozi's businesses: a gym client making a $2,000+ sale in the first seven days is very likely to stay a year; ALAN has three — live and showing stats, first lead shows up, and realising performance beats retainer. | $2,000+ in sales in first 7 days → very high one-year retention. | [OC-08@00:10:29] |
| FRAMEWORK | Monthly referral rate minus monthly churn rate equals your compounding growth rate without advertising. | 10% referring − 5% churning = 5%/month growth. | [LC-11@00:11:07] |
| TACTIC | Choreograph a customer's first 28 days — especially the first 48 hours, when they judge the business — with small promises kept exactly. | First 28 days; judgment within 48 hours. | [LC-11@00:26:25] |
| CASE | At the week-8 feedback call of a 16-week program, clients were offered three years of extra value now, at their current price, if they committed to the higher continuity tier. | $1,000/week during program; built-in continuity ~$500/month; target tier $3,200/month. | [MM-07@00:14:11] |
| TACTIC | Win back lapsed customers with an "I owe you money" message crediting part of their past spend toward a new, bigger service. | 6+ months lapsed; ~200 videos in ~2 days. | [MM-21@00:01:35] |
| BENCHMARK | Even a low-value subscription on a one-time product usually lasts about three months, tripling that customer's LTV — if half of buyers take it, revenue doubles. | ~3 months typical subscription life → 3x LTV; 50% uptake → ~2x revenue. | [MM-26@00:04:06] |
| BENCHMARK | Cutting monthly churn from 10% to 3% more than triples lifetime revenue — conquer churn to get big LTGP. | 10% → 3% churn: $1,000 → ~$3,000+ lifetime revenue. | [MM-26@00:04:56] |
| TACTIC | Give status titles at tenure milestones, placing the first just past your typical churn point and spacing later ones further apart. | Milestones e.g. ~3, 8, 12 months. | [MM-27@00:11:08] |
| TACTIC | Drop the processing fee if the customer gives a second payment method to keep on file — the reduction in involuntary churn exceeds the 3% you forgo. | ~20% churn reduction vs 3% fee. | [MM-28@00:09:53] |
| TACTIC | Make the second payment method ACH (direct bank debit) where possible — bank accounts change far less often than cards and rarely decline. | ACH ~1–2 percentage points cheaper to process. | [MM-28@00:10:53] |
| TACTIC | Offer a lifetime discount that kicks in at your most common churn month, advertise it up front, and count down to it. | Amazon 5% → 15% after 5 months. | [MM-28@00:13:28] |
| DECISION_RULE | Decide the cancellation policy in advance; Hormozi's favourite is a cancellation fee equal to the discount they received. | Fee = discount received (e.g., $600). | [MM-28@00:16:12] |
| DECISION_RULE | If more than 5% of committed customers want to cancel early, investigate the product — fees should nudge people, not handcuff them to something they hate. | >5% early-cancel requests = warning sign. | [MM-29@00:06:55] |
| TACTIC | Once customers no longer have the founder's cell number, tell them exactly where to get help: the channels, the response times, and the people by name. | Example response-time promise: within 5 minutes. | [SC-06@00:18:45] |
| TACTIC | Centralize notes from every touchpoint so the company seems to have one brain and customers never repeat themselves. | ~5 minutes of note review before each call. | [SC-07@00:22:23] |

## sales-process

| type | claim | numbers | source |
|---|---|---|---|
| EXAMPLE | One of a company's top door-knockers of all time refused to stop until he had set 20 appointments, counting each one aloud. | Daily goal 20 appointments set. | [LC-15@00:10:28] |
| TACTIC | Phrase upgrades so the base purchase is implied, and name your lowest package "minimum" so most people take it as the default. | ~90% take a package named "minimum" (his estimate). | [MM-07@00:05:27] |
| PRINCIPLE | The information a prospect needs grows with price relative to their buying power and with how cold the audience is (he says "cool"; probably cold, unclear in audio) — "the bigger the plane, the longer the runway." | $20 → 7-second ad; $7,000 → 30-second ad to a $50M/year owner; ~$500 ad-only ceiling for consumers. | [MM-16@00:03:17] |
| TACTIC | A real strategy call — promising not to take a card — turns qualification into free value, then hands qualified prospects to a salesperson. | Target 25%+ conversion. | [MM-16@00:14:13] |
| SCRIPT | The "magic question" fixes the price first and asks what the client would need in order to be excited to buy, so they design the offer for you. | Example: $3,000 for 3 months to lose 20 lb. | [SC-04@00:03:14] |
| PRINCIPLE | Proof beats promise: whether people believe your promise depends on your proof, so sell paid customers with the results of your free ones. | 1 review at 5.0 vs 20,000 reviews at 4.4 — volume of proof wins. | [SC-04@00:08:47] |
| DECISION_RULE | Hormozi's own practice: he never starts trying to sell until he has 10 or more testimonials. | 10+ testimonials before charging. | [SC-04@00:09:41] |
| DECISION_RULE | If you sell one-to-one, as about 78% of businesses do, fix inconsistent conversions with a setting and closing script; if you sell through a checkout page, optimize the page instead. | ~78% of businesses sell customers one-to-one. | [SC-05@00:05:17] |
| SCRIPT | Pitch in three pillars: boil success down to three things the customer needs, give each a one-line statement and an analogy, and keep the whole pitch to two or three minutes. | Pitch length ~2–3 minutes (vs. a typical 20). | [SC-05@00:06:54] |
| EXAMPLE | Gym Launch qualified prospects as small fitness gyms with at least three employees and at least 30 clients, because anyone else could not run its systems and complained loudly. | Minimum 3 employees and 30 clients. | [SC-06@00:13:32] |
| TACTIC | Add avatar-specific qualifiers to the application on top of BANT so friction matches the narrower avatar. | Gym-owner qualifier example: ≥1 employee, ≥30 members, signed lease. | [SC-07@00:11:06] |
| BENCHMARK | In data from Hormozi's lead-working software ALAN, availability was the number one correlate of companies making more sales. | 15-minute slots, 7 days a week, 9 a.m.–9 p.m. (spanning Pacific to Eastern time). | [SC-07@00:14:50] |
| TACTIC | Use both automated and personal reminders, label the automated ones as automated, and send manual reminders at set times. | A human rep's reminders ~2x show likelihood versus AI-personalized automation. | [SC-07@00:15:39] |
| PRINCIPLE | A lift in show rate raises revenue exactly as much as the same lift in close rate, and show rate is likely easier to move because it is more process-based and less skill-based. | Close rate 35% → 42% = 20% lift; show rate 50% → 80% (achievable with full lead-working) = 60% lift. | [SC-07@00:17:44] |

| EXAMPLE | Hormozi's track record: Gym Launch grew from $6.8M to $37M a year in three years, the businesses were partly sold at a $46.2M valuation, and Acquisition.com's portfolio now does over $200M a year. | Y1 $6.8M/$3M; Y2 $25.9M/$17M; Y3 $37M/$13M; Y4 $32M/$7M; 66% sold at $46.2M; portfolio >$200M/year. | [LC-01@00:11:05] |

| DECISION_RULE | At roughly 1% or 10% of your market contacted you can probably keep doing what you're doing; as you approach 20–30%, maybe start expanding beyond it. | 20K of ~50K contacted; consider expanding when approaching 20–30%. | [LC-10@00:14:49] |

| PRINCIPLE | Scaling stages are defined by headcount, not revenue, because org structure and functions are far more consistent across businesses than revenue is. | 35 employees: $2M restaurant vs $100M software; ~500 employees: very likely able to reach $100M/year. | [SC-01@00:02:45] |
| BENCHMARK | Each stage up leaves far fewer companies: of about 30 million US companies, roughly 24% have an employee and only about 300,000 reach 250–500 people. | 30M US companies; 9% of people start one; 24% have an employee; 3M / 2.4M / 2.1M / 1.2M / 900k / 300k by stage. | [SC-02@00:03:54] |
| FRAMEWORK | Stage 1 Monetize: a one-person business that has made no money yet; the founder becomes a "starter", and graduates by making the first paid sale. | ~30M US companies with ≥$1 revenue; ~9% of people own a business. | [SC-04@00:00:47] |
| FRAMEWORK | Stage 3 Stabilize (1–4 employees): the workload now exceeds the founder's resources, and you graduate by getting help — hiring the first team and giving each function basic structure. | ~24% of businesses have at least one employee beyond the founder. | [SC-06@00:00:00] |
| FRAMEWORK | Stage 4 Prioritize (5–9 employees): the founder becomes a manager of a first fully functioning team, and the overall constraint is trying to be everything to everyone. | ~3M businesses have 5–9 employees, versus ~30M businesses overall. | [SC-07@00:00:00] |
| FRAMEWORK | Stage 5 Productize (10–19 employees): the founder becomes a director, and the core constraint is that customers have nothing else to buy, so LTV:CAC is too low. | ~2.4M businesses at this size (down from ~3M at 5–9 employees). | [SC-08@00:00:00] |
| FRAMEWORK | Stage 6 Optimize (20–49 employees): the founder becomes a leader over two full layers of managers, and the business must grow by doing everything better rather than doing more. | ~2.1M businesses reach 20–49 employees. | [SC-09@00:00:00] |
| BENCHMARK | Only about 3–4% of US businesses reach the 50–99 employee stage. | ~30M US businesses; ~1.2M at 50–99 employees (~3–4%); ~9% of people own a business. | [SC-10@00:01:48] |

## unit-economics

| type | claim | numbers | source |
|---|---|---|---|
| BENCHMARK | Service businesses should run at 80% or higher gross margin — fulfilment should cost no more than $20 of every $100 charged. | ≥80% gross margin for services; $100 price → ≤$20 fulfilment cost; $200 cost → ≥$1,000 price; ~30% net margin target, ~20% COGS. | [OC-06@00:19:44] |
| EXAMPLE | Guarantee math: even if a guarantee doubles the refund rate, the extra sales usually leave you with more net sales — in the illustration, 117 versus 95, a 23% increase. | 100 − 5 = 95 net; 130 − 13 = 117 net; +23%. | [OC-08@00:08:12] |
| BENCHMARK | Earn at least 3x in lifetime gross profit what a customer costs to acquire — and the faster you recover CAC, the faster you scale. | LTGP:CAC ≥ 3:1; ideal payback 1–2 days. | [LC-09@00:01:46] |
| DEFINITION | Lifetime gross profit (LTGP) = gross profit per purchase × purchases over the customer's life. | $15 price − $5 cost = $10 × 10 purchases = $100 LTGP. | [LC-09@00:07:44] |
| CASE | A meal-delivery company's marketers celebrated $100 CAC for $500 customers — but at 10% gross margin each yielded $50 gross profit, a loss on every sale. | CAC $100; revenue $500; 10% margin → $50 GP → −$50/customer. | [LC-09@00:08:45] |
| FRAMEWORK | LTGP above CAC makes money, below loses, and above 3x is a home run to scale; improve the ratio by lowering CAC or raising LTGP. | Ratio >1 profitable; >3 home run. | [LC-09@00:10:19] |
| BENCHMARK | ALAN's data showed CAC within one industry almost always within 1–3x across competitors, while winners earned about 10x more per customer. | CAC spread 1–3x; winners ~10x more per customer. | [LC-09@00:12:11] |

| BENCHMARK | 3:1 is the floor; Hormozi's lifetime return exceeds 36:1, acquisition.com targets at least 10:1 for portfolio companies, and the best run 20:1+. | Floor 3:1; Hormozi >36:1; portfolio target ≥10:1; best 20+:1. | [LC-09@00:14:41] |
| EXAMPLE | A $15/month membership ($10 GP, 10-month stay, $30 CAC) is a healthy 3.3:1 but takes three months to break even, so growth needs debt, investors or savings. | LTGP $100; CAC $30; 3.3:1; break-even month 3. | [LC-09@00:16:35] |
| FRAMEWORK | Two tiers of advertising mastery: tier one is LTGP:CAC above 3:1; tier two is breaking even or better within 30 days, which lets growth compound monthly. | 2:1 in 30 days → ~4,000x customers in 12 months if reinvested. | [LC-09@00:19:16] |
| TACTIC | Lead-getting team return: payroll ÷ engaged leads = cost per engaged lead; × leads per customer = CAC; compare with LTGP. | $100/lead × 10 = $1,000 CAC. | [LC-12@00:10:57] |
